subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES IN CONNECTION WITH PARCEL DELIVERIES OVERSEAS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: BLACKOUT ON APRIL 9-EXTENSION OF LIFE OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY DEPARTMENT
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES IN CONNECTION WITH PARCEL DELIVERIES OVERSEAS
speechtext:
A short time ago the leader of the opposition made reference to representations made by the Toronto board of control in regard to alleged charges in connection with mail for members of the Canadian armed forces overseas. The statement was made that it was estimated that only sixty per cent of the cigarettes sent to Canadian soldiers were reaching destination. I stated in reply that the matter had been brought to my attention; that I had already instituted inquiries and that a full statement would be made as soon as the inquiries were completed.
The representations grew out of a letter written to the Toronto Globe and Mail by Mr. J. D. Cumming, coordinator, petroleum wartime shops, Toronto, and, unfortunately, the Globe and Mail gave this letter undue prominence by writing an editorial in regard thereto before ascertaining whether there was any foundation in fact for the charges made by Mr. Cumming.
In addition, other letters were published and a statement was made by Controller Hamilton of the Toronto board of control which was given wide publicity.
I have no objection whatsoever to publicity when the facts are correct, but I take strong exception to this type of publicity when the statements are made without any foundation or justification. The result is' naturally to create a great deal of anxiety on the part of parents, relatives and friends of boys and girls overseas without serving any useful purpose whatsoever.
I have had the various cases investigated. I am not going to burden the house by reading

Canadian Forces-Overseas Parcels
the results of these investigations. I should like, however, to refer to a few, including the charges made by Controller Hamilton.
Controller Hamilton is reported to have made a statement at a meeting of the board of control on Wednesday, March 24, that hundreds of persons in Toronto had complained of the non-receipt of or tampering with parcels destined to members of the Canadian armed forces' on active service overseas, and that thefts had increased until now it is estimated that only sixty per cent of the cigarettes sent reach them.
I ordered an immediate investigation and, when interviewed, Controller Hamilton could only refer to letters which had appeared in the newspapers, and to ' one other complainant, Doctor W. H. Godfrey of Toronto.
He referred particularly to the letter written by Mr. J. D. Cumming, to which I have already referred.
He simply stated a number of people had expressed the opinion that an abusive practice exists involving the pilfering of articles and parcels and in particular cigarettes, either on board ship or when the mail arrived overseas.
In other words, Controller Hamilton had no specific information to support the statement he made.
Doctor Godfrey was also interviewed. He could give no names or addresses of persons who had complained of having had difficulty, nor could he give any evidence in support of his statement that there were racketeers in the post office who were selling cigarettes in the black markets in England.
Doctor Godfrey at first stated that since 1940 he had put in monthly orders for cigarettes with a certain store in Toronto, to be sent to his son. However, he was unable to produce any receipts in this connection. Inquiry made at the store failed to produce any record of cigarettes having been ordered by Doctor Godfrey or on his behalf, and the manager and other employees of the store were definite in their statements that they had no recollection whatever of Doctor Godfrey or any member of his family having given orders for cigarettes to be sent. This denial by the employees was made in the presence of Doctor Godfrey and two post office investigators.
However, in view of Doctor Godfrey's insistence that these cigarettes had been ordered, and having established that the complete records of such orders for cigarettes are maintained at the store's head office in Toronto, the department had a complete check made of all orders received since January 1, 1942. This check disclosed that one order had been received from Doctor Godfrey. This parcel was
IMr. Mulock.]
ordered on February 18, 1942, and was forwarded through the usual channels. When Doctor Godfrey was interviewed again, he denied having made the statement previously that orders for cigarettes to his son had been put through regularly once a month.
Mr. J. D. Cumming, previously mentioned, having also come into considerable prominence in connection with this matter because he apparently originated the statement that only sixty per cent or less of cigarette parcels addressed to troops were reaching their destination, when questioned about this allegation said that he had oftengiven lifts to unknown soldiers while driving in Ontario. He said that some of these soldiers had already been overseas in this war and that they had complained to him about the non-receipt of tobacco parcels while overseas. One man was said to have told him that he lost about one-third of the packages sent to him. Mr. Cumming admitted his evidence in regard to tobacco parcels was skimpy. He assured the post office investigator that he was not blaming the post office in Canada for any of the irregularities he had alleged existed. With regard to specific mistreatment of parcels, Mr. Cumming was able to give only' one name of an alleged complainant. This involved parcels addressed to a member of the Netherlands army overseas-parcels which, in the ordinary course of events, would not be handled through the Canadian postal corps, but would be dispatched from Canada in the British and foreign mail to England and handled by the British post office.
From what I have said, I believe hon. members will be in a position to judge with what justification the good name of the postal service is being impugned, and Canadians in the army postal service, many of whom are overseas, who are strenuously working long hours in the interests of the efficient handling of overseas mail, are having their characters blackened and their reputations besmirched by some thoughtless and uninformed individuals who make statements without having any evidence to support their charges. Fortunately, this is only one side of the picture. There are letters on file in the post office department from parents and relatives of men overseas expressing their appreciation of the services given under the many difficulties with which they have to contend.
As a matter of fact, the total losses of all parcels for our armed forces and civilians, from all sources, including enemy action, theft, fire and other causes, did not amount to three per .cent. In regard to parcels containing .cigarettes and tobacco, during the year 1942, 2,149,974 parcels were dispatched

Canadian Forces-Overseas Parcels
to the troops overseas. Of this number, 61.889 were lost as a result of enemy action alone, a percentage of 2-87. The number of complaints of non-receipt of cigarettes and1 tobacco parcels, received from all sources during that year, was 3,581. Of these, the department was able to account satisfactorily for 3,547. Either the items were delivered after the complaint was made, or we were able to confirm that they were destroyed as a result of enemy action. This left thirty-four cases to be dealt with which were investigated, and in which the addressee could not be located, did not acknowledge receipt, or for reasons undetermined, the item could not be traced.
I do not for one moment mean to say that we have not had losses, but one of the reasons for complaints was the occasion for the passing of Canadian army overseas routine order 2299. under which no member of the armed forces may receive through the mail more than one thousand cigarettes per month.
Secondly, large numbers of cigarettes are dispatched by certain organizations in bulk, by freight, at the rate of about five million a month, over which shipments the Post Office Department has no control, nor is it in any way responsible for their handling or distribution.
Unfortunately there has recently been a rather heavy loss of parcels due to enemy action, 62,425 tobacco parcels and 29,412 ordinary parcels having been lost at sea since the first of the year. As hon. members of this house will realize, the non-arrival of each of these parcels is naturally a potential source of complaint.
The army postal corps and the Post Office Department maintain a permanent full-time inspection staff, who devote their time and efforts to safeguarding armed forces mail and parcels.
Since this investigation commenced, an article appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 9 under the heading "Charges cigarettes sent troops stolen.'1 This article dealt with an interview given by Captain J. R. Cruickshanks, of the Canadian Legion War Services, who has recently returned from England.	.
A description of this interview was also published in the Toronto Telegram of April 10. under the heading "Private gifts of cigarettes are pilfered."
In this connection I would advise hon. members that, on my instructions, Captain Cruickshanks was immediately interviewed by W. P. Falvey, superintendent of the investigation branch, Toronto. In his report, Mr. Falvey quoted Captain Cruickshanks as stating that in his published interview he was casting no reflection whatever on the Canadian postal corps, either in Canada or overseas, in regard to the handling of packages of cigarettes forwarded by mail or ordinary parcel post, packets addressed to members of the Canadian army overseas. His criticism was of cigarettes shipped in cases and sent by freight, presumably from Canada, and addressed to the assistant, director of auxiliary services in England for distribution to members of the Canadian army overseas. Captain Cruickshanks stated that in making this criticism he had no intention of indicating that the Canadian postal corps was involved in any way. Mr. Falvey further quoted Captain Cruickshanks as stating that he could speak only in the highest terms of the Canadian postal corps, as he had had occasion to come in contact with a postal corps unit which was handling mail for a division of the Canadian army overseas. He spoke very highly of the efficiency with which this unit handled the mail.
Hon. ,J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, I want to follow the statement made by the Postmaster General with a short statement based on inquiries I have made from the army authorities, particularly those overseas, respecting this matter of cigarettes, which has been receiving considerable publicity. I think perhaps it would be worth while for me to take a moment or two in order to explain the position so far as the army responsibility is concerned.
The first point is with regard to the nondelivery or the alleged non-delivery of mail parcels. The parcels are delivered by the postal authorities to the mail orderlies in the units, and then they are distributed through the units according to their mailing arrangements there. I wanted to find out whether there had been complaints fyom soldiers with regard to the delivery of parcels after they got to the units. I cabled the Canadian military headquarters overseas and I received a reply yesterday. It stated that all complaints of non-delivery are investigated and that their records show that bona fide complaints are comparatively negligible and are continually diminishing.
I want to remind the house that roughly over 500,000 cigarette parcels are every three months dispatched and received overseas by post. That checks with the figure given by my colleague the Postmaster General of over 2,000,000 parcels in the year. Canadian military authorities overseas advise that during the first three months of this year, in which there

Canadian Forces-Overseas Parcels
would be approximately 500,000 cigarette parcels sent, there was a total of eight-four complaints received by the army authorities. On investigation seventy-six cases were satisfactorily accounted for and eight cases were not satisfactorily accounted for. I may say that of these eight cases, seven were in respect of parcels which were dispatched not to army authorities but to a civilian agency overseas. That means that so far as the complaints received by the army authorities are concerned, about one parcel in every 60,000 was not satisfactorily accounted for. What I have been dealing with so far is the matter of postal parcels.

With regard to shipments by freight, they are made chiefly through two agencies-the Buckshee fund, which is maintained by the Canadian Legion, and the Overseas Tobacco League of Canada. The shipment of cigarettes in this way, particularly by the Buckshee fund and the Overseas Tobacco League, amount to something like 8,000,000 per month. These cigarettes go to the assistant director of auxiliary services and are distributed by him among the units, from which they are issued free to the soldiers.
This representative of one of the auxiliary service organizations has made the statement to one of the newspapers that there is pilfering in connection with these shipments, and he suggests that the pilfering takes place in transit. The director of auxiliary services tells me that when he was in England there were instances of this kind. These matters are very carefully checked up. The United Kingdom authorities give the privilege of free entry for these cigarettes, and when the United Kingdom authorities at the dock find a box or case showing a certain number of cigarettes on the manifest and then find upon examination of the case that it is short of the number called for by the manifest, they bill the- auxiliary services for duty on the shortage, on the assumption that the shortage has been distributed among the civilian

population and therefore should not have come in duty free. So that they have that way of checking the number.
I have asked the assistant director of auxiliary services, who was in London and is here now, to give me an estimate of the total number of shortages reported while he was there. The figure he gives me is that during the time he was there he does not think there were more than 300,000 cigarettes reported short from these particular shipments. But assume it is a million; even that is a very small fraction of the whole. I have telegraphed Canadian -military headquarters to verify that. I want to point out that this occurred writh regard to the freight shipments and has nothing to do with the post office and nothing to do wdth the army. Even in peace times there is a certain amount of pilfering. Obviously with conditions such as they are in wartime, there are bound to be instances of this kind; and I do not think it will come as a matter of any particular surprise, with commodities such as cigarettes, moving by freight in times like these, when cigarettes are hard to get in the United Kingdom. As will be seen, the number reported missing is insignificant compared with the millions of cigarettes which go overseas. The cases are always reported to the United Kingdom police, and they are most assiduous in connection with it. I know of two prosecutions which were taken, although I capnot inform the house what the results were. One was against private individuals in London who were evidently receivers of some of these cigarettes and had set up an office where they proposed to dispose of them; and the other was against an officer of one of the transportation systems. A Canadian army overseas routine order. This is the order which restricts the number of cigarettes which a Canadian soldier can receive through the mails to one thousand per month.
Formal complaints were received from the Dominions office requesting that steps be taken to stop the sale of cigarettes by Canadian soldiers and stating that traders were

Canadian Forces-Overseas Parcels
alarmed and that United Kingdom treasury was disconcerted. It was suggested that Canadian military authorities issue a general warning that the continued sale of gift cigarettes would prejudice continuance of the concession of duty free entry.
Subsequently, informal discussions indicated1 that the situation was giving further concern, and when the new British tax on cigarettes came in last year, it was pointed out that this would intensify the pressure for illegal disposal. A decision was made to pass this routine order No. 2299 in order to avoid the possibility of black market sales and to forestall the possibility of United Kingdom authorities withdrawing the free entry concession. Canadian military headquarters reports that the situation has been very much improved since the publication of that order.
The order is as follows:
22 July, 1942.
2299-Cigarettes
1.	The privilege extended to Canadian troops in the United Kingdom of receiving cigarettes from Canada duty free was granted by the government of Great Britain on the understanding that these cigarettes were for personal use and not for sale or disposal to civilians.
2.	However, the sale to civilians of these cigarettes by certain individuals has reached alarming proportions, and is jeopardizing the privilege enjoyed by the majority who are complying with the regulations regarding disposal.
3.	In order to ensure that the Canadian army in the United Kingdom continues to enjoy this privilege, no individual, as such, will be permitted, from the date of this order, to receive through the mails more than 1,000 cigarettes per month, which is an ample allotment for any individual.
4.	Consignments of cigarettes will be recorded in each unit, and quantities in excess of 1,000 per month addressed to any individual will be held under unit arrangements. In the event of a move which precludes the transportation of the stock, or lack of storage facilities, the surplus will be turned over by the commanding officer to Auxiliary Services for general distribution.
5.	It is emphasized that the foregoing restriction does not apply in any way to shipments of cigarettes addressed to commanders, commanding officers, officers commanding, hospitals and organizations for distribution to various units and establishments.
I should say that there are also certain freight shipments addressed to officers in charge of formations and units which go direct to the units.
That was the order which was passed, and I am assured by Canadian military headquarters that the excess of cigarettes over the 1,000 per soldier delivered each month is held by the unit on behalf of the soldier himself for eventual delivery to him. They are delivered to the auxiliary services only in the event of
a move which would prohibit transportation of the cigarettes, and Canadian military headquarters advise that moves of the kind are unlikely to take place in the United Kingdom.
The contents of the order were brought to the attention of all troops by publication or otherwise, and our information from Canadian military headquarters is that the troops generally feel that the restriction to 1,000 cigarettes a month is not unreasonable.
In addition to gift parcels to individual soldiers, there is what we call the pool which is formed of the cigarettes I have already mentioned sent by the Overseas Tobacco League and the Buckshee fund, and which amount to something like 8,000,000 cigarettes a month. That is a very small proportion of the number of cigarettes which are used. This pool is supplied by shipments of these two associations; also there are the shipments I have mentioned to the units themselves by local and community organizations.
With regard to the restriction, reference was made in one of the Ottawa newspapers the other day to the United States practice. The United States government supplies, direct, cigarettes for their troops. These are shipped in bulk to Great Britain. The American soldier is entitled to buy at cost price seven packages of cigarettes a week. That amounts roughly to 600 a month, as compared with 1,000 per month which the Canadian soldier is allowed to receive I notice a statement in an editorial in one of the Ottawa newspapers to the effect that the United States soldier seems perfectly satisfied, and the suggestion that Canadian army authorities are likely to urge a similar scheme. I do not for a moment criticize the United States system, which has certain excellent points. On the other hand I noticed an article published in Time of April 12 which was critical of some phases at least of their system, particularly the assortment of brands. The virtue of the United States system seems to be that it is more likely to achieve equality of distribution than ours, but on the other hand under their system the folks back home are deprived of the satisfaction of sending cigarettes to their troops, and there is the further point that the American soldier has to pay for his cigarettes, whereas the Canadian soldier, so long as the present .privilege exists, may get his cigarettes free from generous friends at home.
As will be seen, there are restrictions in quantity under both the Canadian and United States arrangements, and restrictions are bound to be criticized. And I remind the house that that applies not only to soldiers but to civilians. Recently we had an opportunity to purchase 100,000,000 American cigarettes in the

This opportunity gave us a chance to try out a combination of the United States and the Canadian systems. The soldier with generous friends got the benefit of that generosity by getting his thousand cigarettes a month, and to those who did not receive gifts it gave assurance that cigarettes would be available at the duty free price. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the
question asked by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) I should like to give to the house a statement explaining alterations which have just been made on the subject of utilizing the services of conscientious objectors, who are eligible for military training.
Hon. members will be aware that national selective service mobilization regulations (P.C. 10924 of December 1, 1942, and subsequent amendments) provide the procedure under which a mobilization board shall grant a postponement order, in relation to military training, "where the board is satisfied that the applicant conscientiously objects, by reason of religious training and belief, to war in any form and to participation in combatant military .service in which he might be required

Military Service-Conscientious Objectors
to take human life." This definition of a conscientious objector is taken from subsection 2 of section 13 of the mobilization regulations. Subsection 1 of the same section specifically includes Doukhobors and Mennonites as two categories of conscientious objectors especially in view of committals given to members of those faiths by orders in council passed during earlier administration.
Up to the time of the present change in the mobilization regulations, it had been provided that a mobilization board might order any person to whom a postponement order had been granted by reason of being a conscientious objector, to report for "alternative service".
As shown in an answer given to the house as a result of a recent order for a return, a total of 3,401 postponement orders, as of February 3 this year, had been granted by mobilization boards to those seeking to be excused from military training on conscientious grounds.	.
For some time some of the conscientious objectors have been ordered to report for alternative service in certain camps, operated in some cases by the government of British Columbia, in other cases by the Department of Mines and Resources. The province of British Columbia operates seventeen of these camps, for forest protection. The Department of Mines and Resources operates the remaining twelve-two in British Columbia, five in Alberta, two in Saskatchewan, one in Manitoba and two in Ontario-for work in connection with national parks or in other like projects. A total of 1,273 conscientious objectors were working in these twenty-nine camps as of February 3 last.
It will be observed that as of the date referred to, 2,128 conscientious objectors had not been called out for alternative service. This was due to a lack of facilities which might be availed of to place these men at necessary work. And I should like to emphasize that the camps were by no means intended nor operated simply as concentration camps; in every sense they are work camps, performing useful and necessary functions.
In amending the regulations, our main objective was to endeavour to make use in the national interest of the services of all conscientious objectors, and by so doing to provide somewhat more labour for certain essential industries, than would otherwise be available.
The present change in procedures in regard to conscientious objectors, is embodied in order in council P.C. 2821 of April 7th, 1943. This order, passed pursuant to the War Measures Act and the National Resources .Mobilization Act, 1940, amends the relevant
sections of both the national selective service mobilization regulations and the national selective service civilian regulations, and provides for a new procedure under which it is expected that the services of conscientious objectors may be utilized to greater advantage at the present time.
It is now provided that certain officers in the employment and selective service offices across Canada shall be designated as "alternative service officers".
Under existing regulations men who were adjudged by mobilization boards to be conscientious objectors were ordered to one of the work camps where they earned a stated wage of 50 cents per day and board. This had the effect of assigning these men to useful work but on the other hand the effect was to withdraw their services from ordinary industry, farming, for example.
The statement made on behalf of conscientious objectors by those who speak for them is that they are patriotic Canadians willing to contribute their services to the state and make a contribution to the state but that they are not permitted by their beliefs to bear arms.
Believing that on the whole the claims made on behalf of these men are correct, and that they are ready to accept work in occupations where they are most needed, alternative service officers are given authority to direct conscientious objectors to accept employment on farms or in industry where their services are most needed. Conscientious objectors will have the option of refusing to accept employment to which they may have been directed by these officers in which case they will then be directed to one of the alternative service camps.
Any farmer who engages a conscientious objector for farm work, will be required to pay such wage rate'as is fixed by the Minister of Labour which rate will be from $35 to $40 per month depending upon local conditions. Where conscientious objectors are referred to employment in industry, the employer must pay the going rate of wages for the work performed. In either case, however, the men themselves will receive $25 a month, together with board and lodging, while any surplus earned over and above that $25 will be assigned to and paid to the Red Cross society. The arrangement in respect to the camps will continue to be that the man receives 50 cents a day and board and lodging.
As a substantial number of the conscientious objectors are experienced at agricultural work, it is hoped that many of them may become available to the farming industry. It is not

Yukon-Railway Transportation
expected that all of the men now in alternative service camps will be moved out immediately to other employment, although men with special qualifications, who can be used to better advantage elsewhere, will be so moved.
It is anticipated that the change in procedure will result in an addition to our manpower resources available for essential employments, and it is believed that the plan which has been developed will provide a fair means by which genuine conscientious objectors can make a contribution to the productivity of Canadh and thus prove their loyalty.
The plan will be made effective May 1, 1943.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This relates to certain municipalities in northern Ontario which obtain part of a tax on the incomes of certain mining companies. The effect of our law and the law of the province of Ontario, as contained in their taxing statutes, is this. If, for example, a mining company has an income of $3,000,000, it is taxed in this manner. If the company is paying a combined income tax and excess profits tax of forty per cent on its income,
which is the case with the gold mining companies, the forty per cent is reckoned on the income of $3,000,000. That tax would amount to SI,200,000, and that is paid to the dominion government. It is deducted from the $3,000,000, which leaves $1,800,000, which then is subject to a tax, all or part of which goes to the municipality. Let us say that the municipality's share of the tax is two per cent. The two per cent is reckoned on the $1,800,000. which would amount to $36,000.
These taxes, while income taxes, are not greatly distinguishable in purpose at least, and perhaps it would be fair to say not greatly distinguishable in essence, from real property taxes. If the municipalities imposed real property taxes on the property of the municipality, the procedure would be just the reverse; that is to say, the two per cent which I have taken for purposes of illustration would be reckoned on the $3,000,000, which would give the municipality $60,000. This S60,000 would be subtracted from the $3,000,000, leaving $2,940,000, which would be subject to the forty per cent dominion tax.
The effect of this resolution is to do just that, provided that the province of Ontario amends its assessment act in the appropriate manner, so that this is designed to give the northern municipalities a tax on the income of the company before the dominion tax is calculated, instead of after the dominion tax is deducted. That is the effect of this section. It means a loss in revenue to the dominion and a gain in revenue to the municipalities, provided that the necessary amendment is made by the province. I am informed that there is no similar situation anywhere else in Canada. Ordinarily a company doing business in a municipality is subject to municipal tax, which is assessed on something, either the property, the business or something of that sort. It is either a business tax or a property tax. The municipality gets that first; that tax may be deducted from the income, and it is upon the net income after that deduction that the dominion reckons its income tax and excess profits tax.
This question was discussed at conferences between the dominion government and the province of Ontario, and it was not agreed that this would be done. On the other hand, the general principle is that provinces and their municipalities are entitled to impose taxation upon their resources, to tax real estate for municipal purposes-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Last fall we had representa-,Ions from certain mining municipalities of lorthern Ontario pointing out, among other things, that as a result of the dominion's high corporation and excess profits tax acts the taxes payable by mining companies to these municipalities under the provisions of subsections 6,
9 and 11 of section 39 of the Ontario assessment act had been substantially reduced and consequently these municipalities were threatened with financial difficulty, particularly since gold production had been declining. The municipalities therefore requested the dominion to regard the tax payable by a mining company to a municipality under the Ontario statute as a deductible expense for the purpose of calculating dominion income tax and excess profits tax.
At the time I thought we could do this by a ruling of the Minister of National Revenue, since the taxes in question are the equivalent of, or at least are paid in lieu of, ordinary municipal real estate taxes. They are prevented by law from imposing real estate taxes on these mining companies; they cannot tax them at all.
The intention here is to ameliorate the condition of the municipalities in the gold mining centres?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct. I therefore requested my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to have the matter studied. After examination of the Ontario statute the commissioner of income tax ruled1 that this tax on mining companies, although in lieu of the real estate tax, was not a real estate tax but a tax on income. Consequently he was unable under the existing law to regard such taxes as a deductible expense for dominion tax purposes.
. The municipalities, I' believe, had taken the matter up with the Ontario government with a view to securing a change in the provisions of the Ontario statute which would have made dominion taxes paid by mining companies non-deductible for the purpose of calculating the tax payable to the municipalities under the Ontario act. At the time I had some correspondence with the government of Ontario, which was under the impression that someone on behalf of the dominion at the time of the dominion-provincial tax negotiations had agreed that this tax should be regarded as a deductible expense for dominion tax purposes. I could not find any statement by a dominion official or any communication which indicated such an undertaking on the part of the dominion. Nevertheless it seemed that the understanding of the municipalities was justified and I agreed to provide, such an amendment in the forthcoming budget. I may say it was wholly agreed with the provinces that this was not an income tax that they had to discontinue, because it was in its true nature a tax on natural resources or output or something like that. They have similar taxes in other provinces in just a little different form.
Is it not _a tax in lieu of a tax on real estate, to make up revenue?

speechtext:
Yes. This resolution, among other things, deals with the taxing of living allowances. Its purpose is to achieve in the law what has been the government's general policy regarding these allowances, namely, that they must be treated for tax purposes in the same manner as wages and salary. The legislation will extend back to cover allowances received in 1940 and thereafter. This might appear to be unjustifiably retroactive, but I should like to make it clear that its application to the years 1940, 1941 and 1942 is necessary because the government entered into arrangements with a substantial number of employees at the time they were employed to the effect that their living allowances -would be fully taxable as income in all respects as though they were salary. In other cases no specific arrangements with regard to taxation were made, but the persons accepted employment with the government, knowing of the arrangement to which I have referred and fully expecting and intending that their living allowances were to be taxable, and the presumption will be that all persons accepting such employment had that knowledge.
It is fair and right that the persons in both these classes to -which I have just referred should be taxed in 1940, 1941 and 1942 according to these arrangements, expectations and intentions, and it is necessary that this resolution apply so that they will be taxable. Persons serving the government in these years, if they are able to show to the satisfaction of the government that it was their clear

speechtext: Yes. In many cases it was quite apparent from the size of the living allowances that they were not regarded as taxable, that they were regarded as being pure reimbursement for expenses. The fair way to do it would be just to leave it to the income tax division of the Department of National Revenue to tax in accordance with the justice of the case.
Whose word are you to take on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it will work out very well in this way. What I started to say was that that would be the fair thing to do, but of course I could not ask parliament to pass any such general legislation as that, and perhaps it would not be constitutional anyway to leave it to the governor in council to tax this man and not tax that man. On the other hand, it is mainfestly unfair to let all these people out from taxation. I have talked to the odd man myself and said, " What is your understanding? You are getting a living allowance." [DOT] I was talking to one who was getting $25 a day and he said, " I know it is taxable. I know the rule is that it is the same as salary. It is called a living allowance but it is a salary." On the other hand, there are some who should not have to pay the tax.
The only way in which that general situation can be covered, so far as I know, is to tax them all and give this undertaking, that if the governor in council is satisfied that it was their clear understanding that their allowance was not to be taxed, there will be a remission of the tax under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
That is not very satisfactory either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman can think of a more satisfactory method I wish he would suggest it, because I cannot. The question has been canvassed from every point of view and every angle.

I would think that the proper thing to do would be
Income War Tax

this: Drop the present arrangements and start de novo on a clear understanding that all living allowances are to be taxed. Then they can stay or go.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That does not cover the past at all. It does not cover 1942, or 1941, or 1940.
Are there many of these people who did not pay for 1940, 1941 and 1942?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. There are some, I think, who have not, but they have been assessed, and there has been a great deal of discussion back and forth as to whether they are taxable. We have to make a choice. We have either to let them out completely from taxation in cases where it is called a living allowance, on the strength of the Samson judgment, or appeal that judgment, or do what parliament thinks is the right thing to do about the matter. I do not know of any better way than this. In the Department of Munitions and Supply particularly, there are quite a number drawing a living allowance; I do not know how many. But the rule that we laid down early in the war was this, and we thought we had it fairly firmly established, that if a person were here, away from home, and working here for what he said were his expenses while away from home, he could charge his expenses and submit his vouchers, and then he was not taxable at all. He was on a basis of actual expenses.

That is
what ought to have been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is what we encouraged in every way possible. But many did not want to do that on account of difficulties of accounting, or on account of inconvenience. Therefore we laid down as emphatically as we could, and it was well known in the Department of Munitions and Supply and I think in other departments as well, that if they elected to take a flat amount per diem they would be taxable on that as if it were salary. That might turn out to be entirely too much. They might take $20 a day, and it might only cost them $10 a day in expenses. But if they wanted to take a flat amount per diem, the rule laid down was that that was taxable as if it were salary. On the faith of that ruling quite a lot of them, or at least some of them, got their allowance raised. They said: " If it is taxable, I want to be paid on a flat basis. I do not want to be submitting vouchers and sending in bills. Let us have it this way."
Consequently you have on the one hand those who are getting their actual expenses and who are not taxed. Then there are those

who are getting paid so much per diem and are getting taxed and are willing and prepared to pay the tax. Then you have others who did not know anything about it at all but just drifted along or were never told about it, or something like that.
That is a third class.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a third class. So that we have to have some elasticity in dealing with these cases, and the only way we can do it constitutionally, so far as I can see, is to confirm the rule we laid down and then do justice by a remission under the powers of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. I cannot state it in any better way than this. This is not in the law, but it is the undertaking I am prepared to give: That persons serving the government on an allowance, if they can show to the satisfaction of the government that it was their clear understanding that they were not to be taxable on this allowance either in whole or in part, will receive treatment in accordance with this clear understanding under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and these remissions may apply to classes of public servants as well as to individuals.
There are substantial classes of public servants, for example, the employees of the comptroller of the treasury and the employees of the auditor general's office who perhaps get so much per diem when they are away from Ottawa. It is obvious that that allowance should not be taxed. That is more like travelling expenses. They never considered that they were under this rule and they should not be under this rule. Maybe the rule should never have been established; I do not know. But it did seem that the man who was getting $20 a day 300 days a year, or $6,000 a year, should be taxable, just as much as the man who was getting a salary of $6,000 a year, who was working away from home. There were some of these who were in essence dollar-a-year men, who came here at a salary that was fixed to cover what they thought would remunerate or compensate them for coming to Ottawa. Surely we had to tax those on a yfearly salary, also the monthly salaried employees. Therefore we thought that this was the only way we could get this thing wound up.
Then as to the allowance for dependents-
In order to carry out resolutions 1 and 2 you would have to earmark the living allowance as salary, earned income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I wish to say something on resolution 1 if I am in order, Mr. Chairman.

Income War Tax
The minister has brought this matter to parliament and is asking for our opinions and advice. I can agree in a certain measure with what the hon. member for York-Sunbury has said. But I want to point out that I agreed with the minister the other night when he said we cannot practise discrimination. I still think the minister would be better advised to adhere to the arrangements made with these dollar-a-year men when they came here first. They understood that their living allowance would be treated as salary and therefore would be subject to income tax. Others came in later, the minister tells us, without that understanding. I have read that ignorance of the law excuses no one.
This would be ignorance of the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did not turn out to be the law.

Some did not know that this arrangement had been made. I do not suppose that the government went out of its way to tell them that this arrangement had been made, and the employees may never have asked. But there is a condition, and I think if you start to discriminate now between one class and another-and the minister said that there were three classes-you will have plenty of trouble.
The other night, when the question of the farmers paying income tax was under discussion, I said that the farmers were willing to pay their share of the income tax, and I still believe that is true. I noticed in the paper tonight that one hon. member had given an interview to an Ottawa newspaper in which he suggested that indemnities of members of parliament should not be subject to income tax. I do not agree. I am firmly taking the stand that we should not discriminate in favour of anybody. The minister should continue as he did when these men were engaged. Others who came in later should accept the same conditions. If once you begin to leave the matter to the discretion of the treasury officials the difficulty will not be cured; it will be increased, with consequent dissatisfaction all round. Therefore, speaking as a member of parliament, I say that my advice to the minister is to treat them all alike. When someone is receiving $6,000 by way of living allowances each year, as some are doing, besides a fairly good salary from the parent company, perhaps as the president or the manager, he can very well afford to pay income tax on the living allowance. There was a legal decision the other day that they are not subject to this tax. Well, it seems to me that
this is the institution which can, change the law, and if that is the law, it should be changed.
I wonder whether the minister remembers an incident which occurred in regard to the taxation of the C. P. Fullerton estate. As hon. members know, the late Mr. Fullerton got a salary of $30,000 a year as chairman of the board of the Canadian National Railways. He lost the job, but there was a provision in his agreement that he could collect a gratuity, as it was called, of one year's salary if for any reason he should be discharged. He collected his gratuity of $30,000 and was assessed income tax on it. He paid, under protest; the case was taken to the court of appeal, and ultimately over $9,000 of this tax was refunded to the estate. I do not think that sort of thing is justice. That is the sort of thing which makes for dissatisfaction among our people. Many of them get the idea that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor. I would not go that far; but instances like that inspire in the minds of a good many people the notion that there is discrimination in favour of some classes.
In conclusion, I would urge the minister to adhere to the arrangement and carry it through without exceptions. I believe these people should pay income tax on their living allowances.

I suggest to the minister that he submit the other amendments and let us consider this after we have finished the schedule of amendments. Here is one sentence sixteen lines long. It takes about three minutes to read it, and it will take half an hour to dissect it. Let us go on with something else in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right.

legislature * few years ago, when the government of the day introduced legislation while a matter was under litigation, so that the dispute could go only one way,. I thought that was the .most horrible example of abuse of the powers of government that this country ever experienced.
That was in reference to a judgment of Mr. Justice McTague.

Yes. _ I know of a case in New Brunswick in which, while it was under appeal from the trial judge to the court of appeal, the attorney general of the day, who was counsel for one of the parties to the litigation, amended the conditional sales act, and so clinched his case in court; and the judges of the court of appeal used appropriate language with reference to that kind of action. I do not think the parliament of Canada ought to be put in a position where we are doing that sort of thing. I suggest that the minister sleep on the matter. I think it would be very bad legislation. As regards those who came here with the understanding that they were to pay, let them pay; as regards those who had a clear understanding that they should not pay, let us adhere to the arrangement with them. There is a third class of persons to whom the minister has referred, with whom there was no understanding at all. I do not know what you should do about them. I would have to think that over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think it can be worked out with any more justice than it is now.
I wish to say a word first to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. He talked as though the ones who came later did not know about the understanding. Well, for the most part it was the ones who came early that did not know about the understanding rather than the ones who came later, and it would be veiy unjust to tax certain of these people. It is quite obvious, looking at their scale of allowances, that it was designed barely to cover their expenses.

In that case the tax they
would have to pay would not be very large.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; it would not be a very large tax. The governor in council has power of remission under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, but it is not a power which it is desirable to exercise unless parliament knows about it. That is the reason why I am publicly stating here the intention of the government, so that it cannot be said that we are giving remissions contrary to the statute. But the remissions mainly will be in true travelling allowance cases. It is impossible to

draw a line, at least, my advisers cannot think of any way of drawing the line between per diem travelling allowance and per diem living allowance. It is impossible to do so. And it is quite obvious that if accountants in the employ of the auditor general, for example, are getting $5 a day when they are away from their headquarters, because they are away from their headquarters, that should not be taxed. It has been the understanding for years that that was merely a way of estimating their travelling expenses or their expenses when they were in travel status, away from home, and there will have to be remissions for classes of employees like that. For that reason we have made an exception of the members of the armed forces in Canada. I believe the rule formerly was that they received their actual expenses when they were travelling; but then, for purposes of convenience, they were put on a scale; they got per diem allowances. The captain would get so much, the major so much and the colonel so much; but the allowances were reasonable; they were very, very close to what their actual expenses were. Now, rather than say that they must go on actual expenses again, since we have confidence that that scale is all right, we are not going to touch those classes at all. But for other employees in future-and not only other employees of the government but of industry, for it must be borne in mind that this is a general provision-as a war-time necessity we want them to go on actual expenses, not on these per diem allowances, because these allowances may very easily grow into a great abuse. They can be made a way of getting a great deal of salary without taxation. Consequently we say that if they want to go on a per diem allowance, it must be treated as salary, and if they want to avoid that, they may do so by going on actual expenses. It will mean some change in business practice here and there, though not a very great change because the practice is not so very widespread. Most employees in private business are on actual expenses; most of them are obliged to submit their accounts and get their travelling expenses in that way. That is all right; that is not taxable. But if they go into the other realm and get a flat per diem allowance, we say that is regarded as salary and is taxable. With regard to these employees of the government who have been employed within the last two or three years, it will not be very difficult to sort them out. The only solution I can see is to make these allowances taxable for that period and give remissions in cases where we are satisfied that it was the clear understanding that they were

not to be taxable. A great many of them cannot say that. The deputy minister or the minister would know better; he would know that their understanding was that they were to be taxable, and there the law will apply. In other cases there would be remissions.
