This resolution shall be applicable to the income of the years 1940 and subsequent years, but shall not affect any assessments, appeals from w'hich have been lodged prior to April 16, 1943.
How many appeals have been lodged?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know of only one; that is the one that went to the exchequer court.
That was typical of many, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; but I do not think anyone else appealed.
Perhaps they were awaiting the outcome of that appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may have been; I do not know.

I think a good deal of time is being taken up in the discussion of something of which notice has not been given to many hon. members. I think those in the chamber w'ho have not the amendments before them must be very much in the dark with regard to what is going on generally, and I would suggest to the minister that he might bring in his amendments and give hon. members an opportunity to scrutinize them, and then, start at resolution 22, where I think everyone expected we would start.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right; but I w'ish to give some explanation. This resolution will appear in Hansard; hon. members can look at it, and they can also see the argument on it, w'hich will be very helpful in their understanding of it. I do not, however, know the status of the resolution I have just moved. I suppose it is moved and it stands; is that it?
Yes.
It stands as a notice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is not an amendment; it is really a new clause, so that it w'ould have to go at the end of the resolutions we are discussing at the present time,
as resolution 26. H it were possible to make it a subsection it would be different, but that cannot be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very well; that will be resolution 26. Then, on Tuesday, April 6, I gave notice in Votes and Proceedings of certain resolutions, which I suppose will follow along as to number. Let us take this one:
That section 32A of the said act be amended to prevent reduction or avoidance of liability to tax.
That will be resolution 27, and I will move it now.
It is in Votes and Proceedings'!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, as a notice; Totes and Proceedings of April 6.
Can that be moved in committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am moving it now.
Mr. COLDWrELL: Can that be moved in committee? I think a motion has to be moved in the. house, has it not? I am not sure about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know about that; I took it that this was notice. However, I never move these resolutions in the house; I move that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the question raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, these new resolutions do not have to be moved now because they are new sections of the general resolution. They will have to be taken in order, after we are through with the resolutions now before us.
They are part of this general resolution?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then I will move this, which will be resolution No. 27:
That section 32A of the said act be amended to prevent reduction or avoidance of liability to tax.
That does not mean very much without explanation.
Is that all there is in the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is it; that is new resolution 27. Section 32A is as follows:
Notwithstanding any of the provisions of this act, the treasury board may in its discretion determine that any transaction has artificially reduced or would artificially reduce taxation and has no reasonable business purpose other
Income War Tax

than that of avoiding or minimizing taxation hereunder and that no deduction shall be allowed with respect to any expense or disbursement resulting therefrom and the treasury board may determine the extent to which taxation hereunder has been avoided, minimized or prejudiced thereby, and there shall be assessed, levied and paid by any taxpayer such tax as the treasury board may direct and such tax shall be payable as in this act provided.
(2)	In the case of any appeal from an assessment, the court shall have jurisdiction to review the ruling of the treasury board hereunder.
That section is designed to prevent evasion, avoidance or the minimizing of taxation, or the artificial reduction of taxation. There was a section passed in 1938 which was the predecessor of this section, and then this section in its present form was passed in 1940. It gives the treasury board very wide and sweeping powers.

To do
what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To levy taxes, almost. It says:
. . . there shall be assessed, levied and paid by any taxpayer such tax as the treasury board may direct and such tax shall be payable as in this act provided.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	That	is
terrible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It may be. An appeal is provided. Whether it is terrible or not, it is not a very effective section. It cannot be made very effective. There are a good many ways of so transacting business that it is not applicable.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury): Is the
minister proposing to repeal that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are proposing to amend it and to add other sections.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	But	to
retain the principle of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	Well,	I
think that is terrible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like the committee to argue this out. I do not know how far we should go, but I know that with our high rates of taxation the incentive to transact business in such way within the law that taxation is avoided is very great. The long-established principle in the English courts is that a taxpayer is entitled to avoid taxation if he can. If parliament is not clever enough or artful enough to enact legislation which makes him taxable and he can find some way of escaping the provision, he is entitled to do so.
[Mr. Usley.j

That is hardly a fair way to put it. The decisions say that the citizen may be taxed only by clear and express language, and the government of the day, being the father of the legislation and having the carriage of the legislation, must be taken as meaning what it says in its legislation. If they have not drafted the legislation so as to make a man taxable they cannot tax him. To turn round and say that because the government of the day in promoting tax legislation did not use apt language to make the subject taxable, a non-representative board like the treasury board may legislate to impose taxation, violates our conscience. That type of legislation breeds contempt for the law. Necessity makes bad law. For the minister to ask parliament to delegate to the treasury board the power to impose taxation as to the quantum and, I assume, perhaps the rates, and in the absence of the right of the citizen to be heard, is terrible. I cannot imagine parliament doing anything much worse than that, except to legislate to hang a man or to confiscate his property. To tax him without his knowledge or consent when the statute law of the country has said that he shall not be taxed, or a judicial interpretation has been given that he shall not be taxed, and after the act has been before parliament too, is shocking. I wonder who is the father of this idea. This is a star-chamber procedure. To give the treasury board the power to impose taxation is too shocking to think of. If the public understood that these powers were being conferred by . this parliament on irresponsible bodies they would say, what has happened to the mind of parliament? And to make it retroactive is just that much worse. I cannot condemn it any more strongly than that, and I think I carry with me the judgment of every legal man in this house, of every fair-minded man in this house, I do not care where he is sitting. We ought not to give our sanction to this sort of legislation.

I am amazed at the proposal made by the minister. I often disagree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury, but on this I am thoroughly in agreement with him, speaking not as a lawyer but as a student of British history. This is bringing back in another form the old struggle between parliament and the crown, the right of the crown to tax without the consent of parliament. The crown is represented by the minister, and what the government is asking this parliament to do is to abdicate the right for which parliament fought for hundreds of years.

Taxation without representation.

Income War Tax
This is in another form taxation without representation.
This is what the American colonies rebelled against.

This is what the
American colonies rebelled against and I say that a democratic parliament which granted this to the crown-and I am speaking of the crown as represented by the government- would be nullifying the effect of the age-old conflict for the right of parliament alone to impose taxation and to make grants to his majesty.
The bill of rights.

This is a proposal that parliament ought never to consider, on account of its constitutional impropriety.
As far as the other matter which we discussed, the right to tax people on living allowances and so on, this parliament must decide on that, and I agree that living allowances ought to be taxed. But I will not give my consent to losing that right for which parliaments based upon British principles fought for hundreds of years and won after a long and rather bloody struggle. This proposal is a negation of the fundamental right of parliament, and I hope the minister will not proceed with it but will allow parliament-no, I will not say that-I hope the minister will not proceed with it because parliament will not allow him to proceed with it; that is the point. This proposal is entirely wrong, my hon. friend says, from the legal point of view; I say, from the point of view of general history.
And good morals, too.
Will the hon. member state the principle to which he is objecting?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can state it.
Will the minister state where this is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is in the Income War Tax Act, section 32A.
The provision that is being attacked has been in the law since 1940, perhaps since 1938. So that I am not introducing it here to-night. I am reading what the law is, but I must say that I was going to leave it there and I was going to add some sections. I want to be reasonable about this; I do not want to go a bit further than parliament wants to go; I do not intend to try to force anything down anyone's throat. But hon. members have to understand the situation that exists to some
extent and may exist more in the future. I attended one case before the treasury board under the predecessor section. I wish I could remember the facts of that case with sufficient accuracy to state them, but substantially they were these: A company which had ceased to do business had accumulated a large surplus, several million dollars, and the income tax authorities were wondering when that surplus was coming out, because when it comes out it is taxable in the hands of the individual taxpayers. It must be remembered, when we are defending our taxation system, we say that our corporation income tax is heavy. It is a minimum of forty per cent, and 100 per cent under the Excess Profits Act, hon. members know all about that. When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar attacks us because our taxation is not yet heavy enough with respect to corporations our answer is it must be remembered that if the corporation does make too much money-if it does-despite our taxation, when that money goes out to the shareholders, either on liquidation and division of a surplus, undistributed income, or if it goes out by dividends, it is taxed again in the hands of the individual.
And that is double taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for York-Sunbury always refers to it as double taxation.
I do not agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is capable of another interpretation.
When Mr. Euler was minister he brought it in, and he admitted it was double taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is capable of another interpretation. That is what happens. Back in the late thirties or the middle thirties, when the rates on individual income tax were not as high as they are to-day, and when therefore the incentive to employ an artifice to withdraw the surplus free of individual income tax was not as great as it is to-day, the company so arranged things that they got the surplus out without any individual tax. They did it by going to one of the British islands in the Atlantic, incorporating a company, employing intermediaries, and so on, with the final result that $3,000,000 was not there. It was in the hands of the shareholders, and the company and the shareholders were not paying any income tax.
The treasury board under the predecessor 1938 section decided that they would attack that transaction, because apparently there was no business purpose whatsoever, except the avoidance of taxation. Therefore they gave
Income War Tax

notice to everybody concerned-they gave notice scrupulously; there were no star-chamber methods employed at all. All persons concerned appeared before the treasury board. I do not think their counsel appeared with them, but witnesses were brought from those islands in the Atlantic and gave their evidence. Finally an order was made nullifying or in some way reversing the transaction. That section was so weak that we really did not have much power under it. However, they did pay in settlement of that a verj' large sum, by way of taxation. I know it was a very, very large sum. We got that taxation.
Under the gun.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I am not objecting, if they took it out of the country. I have no sympathy with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It may be that that section goes too far. I must say I do not like the sound of taxation being imposed in that way, without some safeguards. It may be that that section goes too far. I invite the views of hon. members in this matter, because I am sure that with the growth of surpluses, as a result of war-time prosperity, there will be many fees paid to corporation lawyers to advise shareholders how to withdraw those surpluses, without the payment of income tax. This is one of the important problems, I may say, before the taxation authorities at the present time.	.
We keep on amending the act, and trying to keep up with requirements. Ever since the act was passed in 1917, ways of legal avoidance would be worked out. And, mind you, there is nothing necessarily immoral about legal avoidance. The courts have given their sanction to it. They have said that anyone is entitled so to arrange his affairs that he may minimize his tax, if he wishes. But these methods are worked out, and it is just impossible for parliament to keep up with them.
Consequently I am proposing certain amendments to this section. I am just giving parliament notice that there is a very important problem here which in some way will have to be met. There are two large problems, the first of which was the matter of depreciation ' about which I spoke the other day. There is the matter of the appreciation, perhaps, of plants which were virtually paid for by the government. The other important problem is the one I have been discussing.
Would the minister read the section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I read the old secton.

Yes.
[Mr. Ilsley.j

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall read what I propose. My proposed section will be placed on Hansard, so that hon. members may study it. I am quite willing to accept any amendment or suggestion which will improve it. But I do say we should not let this year go by without knowing the situation, or giving some thought with regard to this matter. It is not wholly a matter of dissipation of surpluses, but it is to a considerable extent.
I repeat that I want the views of the committee in the matter. I do not mind listening to speeches such as we have heard to-night. It is my view that if there is a defect and if the treasury board is to have powers, there should be safeguards upon the exercise of those powers, and those safeguards should be inserted. The proposed w'ording of section 32A of the Income War Tax Act is as follows:
32A. (1) Notwithstanding any of the provisions of this act, the treasury board may in its discretion determine that any transaction or series of transactions has artificially reduced, or but for the application of this subsection would artificially reduce taxation hereunder, or that its main purpose is the avoidance or reduction of taxation hereunder, either immediate or prospective, and in such case the treasury board may determine the extent to which taxation hereunder has been or, but for the application of this subsection, would be avoided, reduced or prejudiced thereby and in accordance with such determination there shall be assessed and levied upon any taxpayer such tax as the treasury board may direct and such tax shall be payable by him as in this act provided.
That does supply the principle and, to a certain extent, the quantum of the tax; but whether it is still objectionable, I cannot say. The rest of it is new:
(2)	Notwithstanding anything in this act contained, if upon examination of any transaction or series of transactions made directly or through the medium of third parties or the creation of new or intermediary companies, it appears to the treasury board that any payment or benefit in cash or otherwise, received by any person subsequent to the year 1939 as a result of such transaction or transactions has been received directly or indirectly from a company having undistributed income on hand, then the treasury board may find that the main purpose of such transaction or transactions was to reduce or avoid taxation, and it shall thereupon be deemed for the purposes of this act that such person, whether he received any such payment or benefit in the form of capital or otherwise, has received income subject to tax in such year or years and in such amount as treasury board may determine, and tax shall be assessed and levied upon such person and shall be payable as in this act provided.
Any such finding by treasury board may be made notwithstanding that such transaction or transactions may have been entered into either within or w-ithout Canada or prior or subsequent to the coming into force of this section.
(3)	Notwithstanding anything in this act contained, if substantially all of the shares of a company having undistributed income on hand have been purposed by any other company or

Income War Tax
companies, treasury board may find that the main purpose of the sale by the vendor was to reduce or avoid the tax which -would have been paid by the shareholders of such company having undistributed income on hand on the distribution to them of the said undistributed income, and in such case, notwithstanding section 4 (n) of this act, the dividends paid by the company having undistributed income on hand and received by any such other company or companies shall be taxable income of such company or companies and tax shall be assessed and levied upon such company or companies and shall be payable as in this act provided.
(4)	In the case of any appeal from an assessment the court shall have jurisdiction to review any ruling of treasury board made under the provisions of this section.
That is what I was going to propose, subject to any observations that members of the committee might make during the course of this debate which commend themselves to the government.

This is a vepf long
section, and I do not think we can discuss it intelligently to-night. I may say that I agree thoroughly with the minister that methods have to be found to prevent people from escaping taxation. I was one of those who were insistent upon that point several years ago. I think I raised this matter in 1936 as a result of something that came to my knowledge. If we are to decide whether a person is escaping taxation improperly, the only place where this can be decided properly is in a duly constituted court. I think the weakness here is that you are placing in the hands of what is in effect a non-judicial body, a body with practically no responsibility to parliament- the treasury board is responsible to the cabinet -a power which should not be exercised except by this parliament or by a disinterested court.
If we could frame a law so that we can make this-I was going to say offence-a matter which should be decided by the proper court, then I think we are following out parliamentary procedure in the proper manner. As I say, I should like to see the proposed amendment and give some study to it. It is quite long, and it. contains a number of implications. What I said at the outset still stands. I know what the minister said about people setting up companies in Jersey, Nassau, the Bahamas and other places. That went on for a considerable time, and it had to be stopped. But there is a way of doing it. We have complete control over the movement of money in and out of the country, and the physical assets upon which that money is based lie within the borders of Canada. In that way it seems to me that we are protected, pending the decision of a properly constituted court.
As I say, I should like to look into this amendment more carefully than I have been
able to do by just hearing it read. We should be able as a parliament to find ways and means of providing protection, pending what a court would be able to do later, against attempts by persons and corporations to escape obligations they should assume.

I do not
think anybody in this parliament has any sympathy with the procedure adopted by the people in the company referred to by the minister. I think we all frown upon that sort of thing. I cannot understand the patriotism of a millionaire who leaves Canada and establishes himself as a lord down in the Bahamas in order to escape taxation.
Or in England.
In Surrey.

He is
paying much heavier taxes in Surrey, believe me.

That does not
help Canada.

He took it out of
Canada.

I think he helped Canada much more than the hon. member for Moose Jaw did1. But a single case, shall I say of wrongdoing-it is not wrongdoing if it was within the law-should not make us pass bad law such as this. The weakness was that they were not compelled to distribute within a reasonable time the earned surplus. Because parliament perpetrated a weakness by passing a bad statute which was taken advantage of, through legal advice, you are going to turn round and enact a new law to give power to a nonrepresentative body like the treasury board. The thing is absolutely wrong in principle. Let the matter stand so that we can think it over. I should think there would be some other medium outside the treasury board through which this could be handled. After all, what is the treasury board? It is just a committee of the cabinet. The taxing master and the tax gatherer are going to sit on these cases instead of parliament passing a law. That is wrong in principle.

This discussion has been most interesting, particularly since this section in the main has been on the statute books since 1941. I am one of those who have objected consistently to the tendency on the part of this parliament to delegate to administrative bodies the power to determine the rights of individuals in their absence and without giving them an opportunity to present their case. This section is
Income War Tax

in keeping with some of the sections to be found in the War Exchange Conservation Act and the Income War Tax Act. The great danger of this type of legislation is that the servant of the crown becomes in fact the master.
The minister has asked for some sugges-' tions. I think it would be well for him to study the report given to the British House of Commons in 1929 by a committee headed by Lord Sankey. That committee was appointed to look into the whole question of powers delegated by legislation and the effect of judicial decisions by administrative bodies. It was instructed particularly to report on what safeguards were necessary in order to assure constitutional liberty and the supremacy of the law.
The committee sat for a considerable period of time. They took for granted the tendency that has been all too evident during the past few years on the part of parliament to delegate its rights to administrative bodies, to permit the passing of regulations having the force of law and generally to deny access to the courts on the part of his majesty's subjects whose rights have been interfered with. While the discussion was going on, I sent out to get a summary of the report which was made by Lord Sankey, and I think some of the principles enunciated in that report might well be incorporated into this section in order to assure those safeguards which are so necessary when rights are delegated to bodies independent of and not responsible to parliament. Under the section as it n.ow reads discretion rests with the treasury board. True, there is provision for recourse to the courts in the following subsection, which reads:
In the case of any appeal from an assessment the court shall have jurisdiction to review any ruling of treasury board made under the provisions of this section.
That does not give the court the right to determine whether or not the discretion has been properly exercised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is intended1 to.

It grants only the right of appeal against the principle of the assessment. We realize that in time of war, in order to secure the ends that were referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the law must be strictly enforced and there must be no evasion. But if there is one thing that we in this parliament must insist upon, it is that the rule of law shall grant to each and every subject equal access to the courts and equal opportunity to' establish his rights before any body set up by parliament.

I am not going to go into the recommendations in detail, but here is the next one:
There should be supervisory jurisdiction of the high court of justice where there has been any arbitrary or illegal unfairness with private rights.
In order to assure that there shall be no suggestion of the possibility of discrimination being exercised by the treasury board or any other administrative body, a certain rule should be observed. I see in his place the Minister of Justice, the former distinguished president of the Canadian'Bar association, an institution which throughout the years has stood firmly for the necessity of upholding the rule of law in the face of a tendency on the part of government gradually to recede from its application, gradually to legislate for parliament, and in process of time to place this country in a position where the major portion of its legislation does not come before parliament but comes before administrative bodies independent of parliament. It may be said that the minister and the government must answer for the acts of these administrative bodies. But in essence the servant set up by the crown becomes the master of the individual in the decisions that he makes.
I will refer to just' one or two more of the recommendations by Lord Sankey's committee:
1.	In future legislation parliament should proceed on the principle that no minister (in which word we include any officer of a minister acting under his orders) should give a judicial decision in any dispute in which the minister has a kind of departmental interest. If such cases appear likely to arise, parliament should provide for determination of the dispute by a ministerial tribunal functioning independently of the minister.
Certainly bodies such as the treasury board do not function independently of the minister within the terms of what this committee has in mind.
2.	Each of the parties to a dispute should be given the opportunity of stating its case-not necessarily orally-and should also be given the opportunity of knowing the case which it has to meet and of answering that case if it can.
There is no suggestion anywhere in the original section or in the amendment proposed by the minister this evening that he will grant to the individual the right to have his side of the case placed before any body.
3.	Any party affected by a decision should be informed of the reasons on which the decision is based.
This is one of the most fundamental rules that we as a parliament are gradually abrogating. We are certainly abdicating our rights in not insisting that each party to a decision

Income War Tax
rendered by a government tribunal shall be made aware of the reason for the decision. Often to-day we have decisions made by these various war-time boards that have been set up which interfere with private rights, interfere with the small business men, take away their rights and then deny them the right of recourse to the courts. Against that tendency I protest. In every case where a decision is made by a government board affecting the right of the individual I believe that parliament has the right to demand that that decision shall be subject to appeal to the courts. We have had these decisions on every hand made by the various boards that have been set up, boards in the munitions department that take away individual rights, that say to one member of a class that he shall have certain rights and say to other members of the same class that they shall not have the same rights. If out of this debate this evening there should come a determination on the part of this parliament to insist on behalf of the people we represent that from any decision of a war-time board or any other administrative body set up by this government which takes away an individual's rights or interferes with his livelihood, which takes away not that individual's rights as a member of a class but his own individual rights independent of his class, there shall be the right of appeal to the courts, then I think this debate will have been worth while.
Finally, Lord Sankey recommended:
4.	Such a decision should be in the form of a reasoned document available to the parties affected. This document should state the conclusions as to the facts and as to any points of law which have emerged.
This principle enunciated in 1929 and accepted by the British government of that day and by all succeeding governments there is denied every day in this dominion, not only in matters particularly affecting the war but in matters of business which by no stretch of the imagination can be considered to contribute in any way to the winning of the war. Practically the sole voice raised anywhere in this dominion against this practice has been the voice of the Canadian Bar association. It has often been said that we have in this house a large representation of lawyers. Throughout the ages lawyers in parliament regardless of their political affiliations have insisted on the rights of the individual. We as lawyers in this parliament week in and week out have seen the gradual diminution of the powers of parliament and the gradual whittling down and denial by administrative boards of the right of the individual of appeal to the courts when there has been interference with private rights. But very few have raised their voice against
that tendency. If out of this debate will come a determination on the part of the members of this house to insist that its rights which mean so much to any member of a British parliament shall not be abrogated, except where necessary in the interests of the security and safety of the state, something worth while will have come out of the discussion here this evening.
I need only conclude with the words of Mr. Chitty, editor of the Fortnightly Law Review, who in the last few months has been dealing with interferences with private rights and with the gradual diminution of the powers of parliament by a parliament that has not stood up for those rights. Only the other day he made this statement:
It may be necessary to set up certain controls by which the parliamentary sanctions are administered, but not dictatorships such as we have to-day, for which as the chief justice has said-
That reference is to the Chief Justice of Canada and the judgment he gave with reference to the chemical controller:
-parliament is responsible, but which clearly show that they acknowledge no responsibility to parliament. One has only to point to England-perhaps not a popular example-to show' that even in w'ar time parliament can still function and exercise the necessary control without the interposition of dictatorships to institute and administer those controls.
I have not the judgment of the supreme court before me, but I invite hon. members to read it. Take the judgments of Chief Justice Duff, Mr. Justice Davis and Mr. Justice Rinfret. They accept as legal the set>-ting up of controllers in war time under provisions contained in the War Measures Act. They indicate that unless there is a scrutiny, a care, a determination on the part of parliament to assure that private rights shall not be destroyed by controllers set up and uncontrolled by parliament except through the route of ministerial responsibility, we approach a position dangerous to the welfare of parliamentary government in this dominion.
There is one other course which the minister could follow. One hon. member suggested the other day that orders in council should be submitted to a committee of parliament for the purpose of considering them and recommending changes. I do not agree with that. I believe that the tendency toward order-incouncil government has arrived at a point where the government to-day, when it does not wish to bring a matter before parliament, takes the easier course of passing an order in council determining rights, setting up offences, and creating responsibilities. We members of parliament accept what is done without objection.

Income War Tax
We have another thing coming up at the present time, in connection with debt adjustment in western Canada. The Minister of Justice said the other day: What we will do is this; we will amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act by making it applicable to Manitoba as well as Saskatchewan and Alberta, and then we will pass an order in council setting up the machinery, such as it is, creating rights, because parliament is too slow, too dilatory. That is what I gathered from the minister's remarks.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Will the hon. member allow me to correct him on that point? What I did say was that there would be an order in council passed now to enable the courts to grant staying orders in the land debt cases, and that there was being prepared a bill to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to make it a more effective instrument, and to extend its application to Manitoba as well as to the other provinces; that that measure would be introduced as soon as possible after the Easter recess, for the consideration of parliament; and that an order in council to enable the courts to render valid staying orders in the form provided for hitherto by, I think 't is, section 15 of the civil rights act of the province of Saskatchewan, would be passed so that it might be available immediately and might stay or permit the courts to stay, if it were thought necessary, the avalanche of actions which, the hon. gentleman said in the house some time before, was preventing effective agricultural production in the western provinces.

The words of the hon. gentleman are these, as reported in Hansard at page 2097:
I understood there was some urgency about this, and my experience during the very short time I have been in this house is that when matters are urgent it is sometimes inconvenient, for those who require them, to have them delayed until they can be dealt with in the form of a bill.
Read further on.
The hon. gentleman should read it all.

That is exactly the point I make. Members of this government, instead of submitting legislation to the house where it could be debated, are gradually arriving at a point where action is taken by order in council and parliament is not consulted at all. My suggestion is this. Since there is no hon. member, no matter what his position, who can say with reasonable certainty what the law is on any of the subjects dealt

with by order in council, there should be a committee of this house set up for the purpose, not of changing orders in council which are passed, but of placing before parliament from time to time the record of the orders in council which have been passed which interfere with private rights, which depart from time-honoured principles of legislation, which deny rights to one individual while granting them to another, to the end that parliament will at last have supervision over legislative action taken by the various boards and controllers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know it is my duty to follow the hon. gentleman in his general attack on the system of organizing the country for war. There has to be a certain amount of what might be called regimentation, I suppose, w'hen a country is at war; and things have to be done when a country is at war that would not be normally done in times of peace. The hon. gentleman did not show in his speech any awareness that there was any necessity for a different organization in time of war from that in time of peace.
Oh, yes. This is the point I made, that many of these boards pass regulations which have no possible connection with the winning of the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, that is only an assertion. I should like to have some instances before I would assent to it. It is easy to make, but it is difficult to prove. It sounds well and perhaps would command some assent from persons who resent too many restrictions and controls. But the hon. gentleman must understand that to build up a country's war organization as rapidly and as far as has been done in Canada requires us to make very rapid changes in our system of organization of the country's industry and trade and business. The control of prices, of supplies and of industry in such a way as to turn them from peace-time activities to war-time activities means a great deal of clashing with individuals who w'ould like to do something which would be a little more profitable if it were left to themselves. There is no way that I know of whereby that can be done without the vesting of a large amount of power in the hands of officials. As I said to the house one day, parliament cannot do it itself. I would point to the fact that parliament has been in session now for nearly three months, and the amount of actual deeds of parliament, of action taken by parliament, is not very great. It has had a different value, and a very considerable value, but it has not lain in that direction. It is necessary, if the tremendous volume of necessary business, acts,

Income War Tax
decisions, one after the other, day and night, is to go forward in proper sequence, that an immense amount be done by order in council. As I told the house, I believe, a while ago, about 12,000 orders in council were passed last year. Did we pass 12,000 orders in council to get ahead of parliament or to keep business away from parliament? Did we do it because we enjoyed the work that was necessary in getting all that business through? Not at all; we did it because decisions had to be made and action had to be taken. It had to be taken every hour of every day, every day of every week, every week of every month, and every month of every year. The war will not wait; that is all. When we get into more leisurely times; when, instead of having an expenditure of 85,500,000.000 a year, we have an expenditure of 8500,000,000 or 8600,000,000 a year again, we can refer a very much greater volume of business to parliament. We did not do these things because we did not want to bring these matters to parliament. Why, we bring everything we can to parliament. Unless I am greatly mistaken, an hon. gentleman suggested action by order in council in reference to debt legislation; at least one hon. member opposite did. It was suggested that the matter was so urgent, that these farmers in the west were threatened by creditors to such an extent, that action should be taken in this way. It may have been the hon. member for Weyburn-
I believe I did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, some hon. gentleman suggested that action should be taken by order in council. Could we have taken action by legislation? When would our legislation have been introduced, and when would it have been passed?
You have not passed the order in council yet, although it is so urgent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But we can pass it. Does the hon. gentleman say we should wait for legislation? I should like to have his view on that. Does he want us to wait until legislation can be introduced and passed after the Easter recess, to deal with that matter?

I could understand perfectly well that if there were urgency and an order in council were passed and put into effect immediately, there could be no objection, if the legislation were introduced afterward. But where is the urgency? The judgment has been handed down for several months; the opportunity has been before parliament and the government for several months to introduce legislation. The reason
given by the Minister of Justice was that he had not been able to consult with the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has evaded the question; he has not said whether he would like us to deal wth this particular matter by legislation rather than by order in council. If he really wants the matter dealt with, he wants it dealt with by order in council, because it certainly would not be dealt with for months by legislation, even if we introduced the bill. There are certain matters that can very properly be dealt with by orders in council, and certain other matters that have to be dealt with by controllers' orders and boards' orders. Everyone who has any appreciation of the practical phases of the war knows that this must be the case.
That does not have much to do with the matter before the committee, but the hon. gentleman was attacking the actions of civil servants or administrative boards, saying that we must not set them up and put them above parliament so that parliament loses its control. The principle of this proposal is that a committee of the government, which is not an administrative board in any sense, but a committee of the government which is responsible to parliament, should go into these transactions and make an assessment on certain principles which are set out in general form in this section, with an appeal provided to the courts. The hon. gentleman says that the courts cannot review the discretion of the treasury board. The ruling of the treasury board is a discretionary ruling, and it is expressly provided' that this ruling is reviewable by the court. This matter was debated in this house in 1940, when subsection 2 of section 32A was added. The clear understanding was that the court was to be able to review the discretion of treasury board. It is now suggested that the matter be referred to the courts and that the courts make the assessment. There is a difficult task involved here. First, there is the difficulty of ascertaining how much income has been avoided and in what years, and then an assessment of tax in respect of that income. Before you can get it into court I think someone has to do that work; I do not think the court can be expected to do it. I believe a preliminary hearing by some tribunal is necessary.
As I say, however, I should like to hear the views of hon. members on the principle and the provisions of the section, because we should put something in the bill. It is a problem, I am telling the committee. A great many of these surpluses in the hands of individuals will decline and perhaps eventually
Income War Tax

disappear without taxation unless something is done. For years the commissioner of income tax has advised that it is impossible to foresee or envisage the methods that will be adopted, and that the only possible way of dealing with the matter is to express general principles and leave it to some tribunal to decide. I do not care whether it is the treasury board. If hon. members would like to have it done by one of the boards that the hon. member for Lake Centre loves so much, I could give it to one of them. But I should think the treasury board' would be more responsible to parliament than an outside board. Somebody has to be entrusted with the duty of watching these transactions, determining how much tax is avoided and whether the main purpose was to avoid taxation. If the main purpose was not to avoid taxation; if it was a legitimate business purpose, then the transaction should not be impugned. But the treasury board should have the power to make that finding where the main purpose was to avoid or minimize taxation and then make an assessment, and let the people concerned appeal if they wish to do so. If it is a glaring case, I imagine they will not be likely to appeal, but if it is an honest case they will appeal and the courts can uphold or reverse the action taken by the treasury board. I edn tell the committee that there is a great problem here which has to be dealt with in some way.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to much legal argument here to-night. Stripped of all these legal points, is the situation not simply this? In the ordinary course of events, when an individual makes an income tax return, if the commissioner of income tax does not believe it is a proper return I understand he assesses that individual, and thereupon that individual either pays the assessment or goes to the exchequer court. Is that not the situation? Under those circumstances, if these companies are trying to avoid something, instead of the commissioner of income tax making the assessment the treasury board makes it, and the company concerned can go to the exchequer court. I may not be right in that, but I thought that was the procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commissioner informs me that the income tax division does not make arbitrary assessments; it gets some evidence upon which to make its assessments before doing so. Perhaps that is what the hon. gentleman means.

But they make
the assessments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They make the assessments.

And if an individual wants to appeal from the assessment he can go to the exchequer court. In this case, instead of the officials of the department making the assessment, which is how it is done in practice, the treasury board is to make the assessment on these companies, and if they do not like it they can appeal to the exchequer court. I do not know why we need all this legal argument about the matter. If we use a little common sense ini regard to it we shall get along faster.

In the
one case the commissioner makes the assessment under the sanction of law, as laid down by parliament. In the other case the assessment made by the treasury board has not the sanction of law.

We are trying
to give it that, are we not?

I do not
know what we are trying to do.

Would it not be possible to enact legislation which would make it a crime under the law to evade taxation? If the penalties were sufficiently severe, that would be a deterrent, whereas it seems to me that to-day it is just a sort of game as to how you can get out of it, and when you are assessed you pay only a small penalty by way of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would be much harder
to draft a defensible section creating a crime, making the avoidance of taxation a crime, than it was to draft this section. We must not lightly make things crimes. It is not a crime, has never been regarded as a crime so to arrange one's affairs that taxation can be avoided. It is something that should not happen, and the taxation should be obtained, but start to draft a definition of a crime there and you will find yourself in great difficulty. I should have a great deal of sympathy with what the hon. member for York-Sunbury said in respect of that, because it would sweep in transactions that are all right, that are not even undesirable. I do not think you could draft a definition in such a way that it would not.

Let this
stand.

The amendment is lengthy.
I thoroughly agree that not only hon. members of the opposition but some on this side of the house would wish to discuss such an

Income War Tax
important and lengthy amendment. I certainly caflont agree with members of the opposition who suggest that it is in contravention of magna chart-a, the bill of rights and almost the rights of man. I think that is absurd, and there is no such suggestion in the amendment in any shape or form. As the minister pointed out, we have of necessity to stream-line our machinery of government so that it will work effectively. I presume that will be the case not only during the war but for at least a considerable period after its termination. Therefore, so far as the method suggested is concerned, namely, delegation of a certain power by the government or by this parliament to the treasury board, I see no great conflict with many other acts that we have passed not only during the war but prior to the war and will continue to do after the war.
I feel, however, that the amendment requires careful reading and consideration. I suggest to the minister that since there is a retroactive provision in it, there can be no immediate urgency for having this passed to-night or even before the Easter recess. I think it would be time well spent and the mind of the minister would be better satisfied if hon. members could have an opportunity in the quiet of their rooms to study the provisions in detail and form an intelligent opinion regarding the measure.

That in order to make possible the use of a simplified return and facilitate the calculation of tax by all individuals (except proprietors and partners in any manufacturing, trading or merchandising business) in receipt of incomes for 1942 from all sources not exceeding $3,000 and not in receipt of investment incomes of more than $1,500, such individuals shall be subject to the appropriate amount of tax set forth in

speechtext: We are debating them?
We should not be, but we have to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suggest No. 29 be one of which notice has not been given. It is simple:
That the information return required to he filed by employers showing the amount of salaries or other remuneration paid to persons in their employ in the preceding calendar year and the amount of tax deducted at the source
Income War Tax

under the provisions of the act from the salary or wages of such employees shall in respect of the 1942 taxation period be filed on or before the 31st day of May, 1943, and in respect of all taxation periods subsequent to 1942 shall be filed on or before the last day of February in each year.
I do not know the reason for that or the explanation.
It is a matter of administration. Let that stand with the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right.
Now I suggest that No. 30 be the one relating to merchant seamen. That is found in Votes and Proceedings of April 6. It reads:
That any amount received by an officer or man of the merchant marine as bona fide war risk bonus in accordance with the usage of the merchant marine, and any value of board or lodging on shipboard received by such a person while performing services in respect of which war risk bonus is payable, shall not be considered as income subject to tax under the Income War Tax Act.
I do not know whether it requires an explanation now; I am merely giving notice.
I think that is understood.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may add that there may be further development of it in the act.

I wash to take only about ten minutes to place before the committee certain circumstances regarding certain Canadian members of the flying personnel of the Royal Air Force ferry command. These men are engaged in flying aeroplanes, bombers, land planes and so on from this continent to the British isles. They are being charged income tax, and their basis of claim or their contention is that they should be totally exempted, like all those in the armed services, who are described as being on active service overseas. Certainly I maintain, and I do not think it can be contradicted, that that description applies also to the men about whom I am going to speak.
They are regarded for taxation purposes as civilians, although many of them wear uniforms, because they are compelled to do so, and they are all trained to use guns. There are guns on the flying boats. They have been attacked in the air by enemy aircraft and by enemy anti-aircraft guns. This indicates the danger of attack and the liability, if captured, of being treated as guerillas. But normally they appear to be recognized only as civilians. Members of the Royal Canadian Air Force, the corresponding body in Canada and on the other side, are exempt from taxation when overseas or on the Atlantic, and even on the Pacific. Resolution 22, which I understand we are now dis-[Mr. Ilsley.l
cussing, provides that if such men are outside Canada they shall pay no tax for doing work ordinarily performed in the air or in watercraft.
I have said that they are constantly open to attack by enemy craft, both enemy aircraft and anti-aircraft guns. That surely constitutes war	risk.	They	are also subject to	whatmight be called flying risk, extra to ordinary war	risk.	And	that is	greater than anycomparable operation, because they are flying a long route from this continent to Great Britain. They have the added risk of flying new	boats	on such long	trips, almost	theirfirst	flying	trips.	These	boats might	quite
readily develop unforeseen and unexpected flaws, which would leave them out in the middle of the Atlantic. When they are put down there, their fate is doomed. There is no recourse and no rescue in a situation of that kind. There are no landing fields at intervals of fifty miles, as there are in land flying.
The loss of their personnel is deeply significant of the importance and the danger of their operations. It cannot be calculated exactly to a percentage, but it is something like thirty-five per cent of loss of personnel in two years. That is a tragic record, and I believe it is not comparable with any other field of active service.
Then, there is the other side of the picture. It is true that they are paid what might be considered a large salary, which is supposed to cover all risks. But it does not do so. At the time of the origin of this service there was no time to train men. It would have taken many months, or a year or two to do so. Men had to be secured quickly. The government had to get fliers in a hurry, and they had to take just what they could get. The result was that they picked up a large number of what are known as bush fliers, men who had had long experience, painfully acquired experience, in building up a fine record in connection with flying supplies into the north country, or into the mines in the northern parts of Ontario and Manitoba. The government had to pay above the standard civilian rates, on account of the extra risk involved. Possibly the men who were hired did not understand-indeed, perhaps no one could then understand-what their actual risks might be.
I should like to point out at this stage the difference between hiring a fully experienced airman, with years of experience behind him, lots of flying in the north country which called for the development of the greatest degree of initiative and enterprise on the part of the airman, and the man such as the raw

Income War Tax
recruit on which the government would have to spend money for the purposes of giving one or two years' training. What would that experienced bush flier be worth, as compared with the recruit whose training would require a year or two? It would be just like the army picking up a first-class doctor, and comparing his services, ability and experience, acquired over long years, with those of a man who has come in as a medical orderly, or who worked in a hospital.
Or, if I might put it in this way-if such a thing were possible-the difference would be the same as that which would exist between recruiting a general with all his training and experience, as compared with recruiting the ordinary private soldier. That would be a fair comparison.
It developed that the risk was greater than had been expected, not only from the point of view of attack, but because new and untried planes were used. Again, there is no pension for the widow or the children of these men. Any insurance they have is held at their own expense. To provide a very moderate pension would require insurance to the extent of something like $15,000. And the rate of premium is so high it would require payments of something between $1,000 and SI,200 a year. All that must come off his .pay. The insurance that he would get is of such a nature that it could not be taken off the savings portion of his income tax.
Of course they are provided with no ration allowance while in Canada, no living-out allowance, no allowance for a wife, no allowance for children, no medical care and no dental care. And if they are sick their pay stops the minute they become sick, or meet with an accident. All responsibility for and the results flowing from an accident or sickness must be borne by the man himself.
Another and perhaps greater line of dissatisfaction is the discrimination between two different men who belong to the same command, doing exactly the same kind of work and sharing the same risk. There is nothing more calculated to promote friction than to have two men doing the same thing, one of whom is treated entirely different from the other.
When this work was first started it was necessary, as I have said, to get men in a rush, not only Canadians, but Norwegians, and men from the United States. They were all eagerly picked up and taken on. I hold in my hand a copy of the contract entered into between the air command and the employees who, in this instance, were citizens of the United States. I should like to quote only one paragraph from it. Let me explain 72537-142
again that this is the exact contract made between air command authorities and an employee of United States origin. It reads as follows:
In the event that .the employee is a bona fide citizen of the United States of America and a non-resident of Canada, the employer-
That is, air force command.
-shall indemnify the employee against aqy and all claims for British or Canadian income or national defence taxes in respect of the remuneration to be paid to the employee hereunder and shall reimburse to the employee, upon demand and proof of payment wherever required, the full amount of any such taxes in respect of such remuneration as may be deducted or withheld therefrom at the source or which he may otherwise be legally obliged to pay.
It does not require anyone with even a superficial knowledge of legal terminology to understand that. It is clearly expressed that when these United States citizens were taken on and signed the contract they were entirely indemnified against having to pay income tax either for British or Canadian sources. And as a matter of fact they do not pay it. As a matter of fact they do not pay anything out. I do not know who pays it, but it is not paid by them and they do not pay any United States income tax either. That provision is not in the Canadian contract. I have not the Canadian contract before me, but I am satisfied that that clause does not appear in it. The fact that our men have to pay a tax constitutes an unfair discrimination as between two classes of men doing the same work.
There is another factor that should be considered which places an unfair burden upon these men. Many of the Canadian flying personnel are sent down to work at the R.C.A.F. ferry office at Nassau. There is no price control or rent control in Nassau. Prices have sky-rocketed and living costs are from seventy to eighty per cent higher than in Canada. No subsistence allowance is made to the Canadian men when they are sent there. This may seem a minor grievance, but it is important to these men.
I submit that all this makes a good case for the exemption of the Canadian men from income tax, especially when it is realized that the United States men are protected by their contracts from having to pay any income tax. It will be said that they get a large salary which is intended to cover all these risks, but I submit that their salary is not high enough to cover the extra risks involved. It may be argued that it covers some of them. I wish to be absolutely fair and I think there is some argument that part of their salary should and

Income War Tax

is, as a matter of fact, considered as compensation for the war risk. In fact, it is so expressed. I would suggest that the government decide what proportion of the civilian pay is intended to cover.war risk and how much for insurance, and then permit these men to credit these sums against their ordinary income tax.
I dp not think anyone can deny the justice of this claim. This is a minor concession, but it would help these men considerably. The loss of revenue would be trivial, because I think the total personnel is under 200 men, something like 178.
It is suggested sometimes that the habit of the Minister of Finance is to railroad his bills through, regardless of any representations that might be made. Some people may concede that it is his duty to get his bills through without any change. At the same time he has shown a readiness in the last day or two to make adjustments where necessary, provided, as I understood him to say, they did not interfere with the main policy of raising revenue.
In this instance I suggest that we would not be deviating from the policies he has laid down. There never has been a measure of finance, certainly no measure that amounted to anything, which, if it were based on straight policy, did not create incidental injustices here and there. I think our duty is to point this out and to ask the minister to look into these matters and smooth off the bumps, so to speak. That is the purpose of this discussion. If he gave his sanction to this, he would in no way deviate from his main line of policy. If it was a question of an enormous reduction in revenue, I could quite understand that he could not be expected to agree to that, but this is a small thing.
The obligations and satisfactions of mankind are generally made up of small things. A thing like this may appear small when considered in the light of the budget, but it is most important to these people. I should like the minister to give me an assurance that he will look into this and see if he cannot adjust these grievances.

I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has just said in regard to pilots of the ferry command. He gave a figure of about 200, but there are actually 330 men engaged as pilots, co-pilots and radio and flight engineers. Of that number there have been 121 casualties in two years, making the losses something around 19 per cent per annum. Their insurance rates are exceedingly high, and all most of them can get is accident insurance, the premium for which runs about 9 or 10 per cent

if it is to cover duty in different parts of the world, and about 6 per cent if it is to cover flights to the old country.
I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member that the minister should allow that portion of the salary paid to these men which might be considered as war risk as an exemption from income tax. I have talked to these men and I know something of the work they have been doing. They are in danger every time they fly. Sometimes they go right in behind the troops with supplies, at times without any great protection. Certainly, if any men should get consideration from the income tax division, it is these ferry command pilots of Canadian origin.
Are they residents of Canada?

Yes, but sometimes they have to set up temporary residence in Nassau or in other ports. As my hon. friend has said, there is no income tax to speak of in Nassau, but there are very high taxes on food, rent and one thing and another. Where a man has to maintain a home here and keep himself there, he finds himself up against the income tax here and greatly increased costs of living there. I think every consideration should be given to these men, and I am sure the minister will give it.

I should like to support what has been said by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I think these men have a very real case. I do not intend to go into the matter in detail to-night, but I should like to point out that recently there was another casualty list which brings the number up to that given by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. This was from a Catalina flying boat on the way from Africa to Great Britain which was intercepted by the enemy and destroyed, all the men being lost. The minister and his department will note that the casualties in this service have been exceedingly high. The number of personnel was given by the hon. member for Moose Jaw as 330, and there have been casualties of 121. This does not mean that only 330 men have been employed in this service in the last fifteen or eighteen months, or whatever it is, but that the average on strength throughout that time has been 330. After all, that is the number we should take. Men drop out to go into something else and are replaced by other men. You have to take the average number engaged in the particular work over the period of time. During that time 121 have been lost. When compared with the men in the Royal Canadian Air Force who hold comparable ranks, after deducting income

Income War Tax
tax and adding what the Royal Canadian Air Force men receive-they deserve every nickel they get-by way of subsistence and other allowances; after allowing for insurance costs, several categories of men in the ferry command are getting less than the men in the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Do they get pension benefits and the like? [DOT]
They have no pension benefits whatsoever.

And no medical
benefits?

I do not disagree; in fact, with the general principle I agree, but for clarification may I ask the hon. member if it is not a fact that the ferry command is not exclusively under our control? The United Kingdom has something to do with it?

I think it is exclusively under the control of the United Kingdom. But these are Canadian boys domiciled in Canada, and that is why we have the right to tax them. They are working for the R.A.F. ferry command, but they are Canadian citizens who are technically domiciled in Canada, and therefore as citizens their incomes can be assessed for income tax just like all the rest of us.
I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was quite right. These boys are not anxious to escape any obligations which they should properly assume in the war. But if it is argued,
as it sometimes is argued, that the rate of pay which was granted to them was in some degree
to compensate them for the war risk they assume, it seems to me that they have strong grounds for asking that that portion of their pay which is to compensate them for the war risk they assume should not be assessed for income tax purposes. I think that is a perfectly sound request on their part. Indeed, I would go further and say that on account of the shortness of the life and the fact that many of these men are married and are too old to be enlisted in the regular R.C.A.F. the minister should consider exempting them from income tax entirely. But if he will not do that, certainly a case can be made out for exempting from income tax that portion of their pay which is to compensate them for the war risk they assume on this work. If that were done I believe it would be a measure of justice, and they would deeply appreciate it.
A number of other members of the house know of these cases. I met one of these young men from my own province on the train one day, and that is how I came to learn about this. I can assure the minister that as far as we in this group are concerned, if he grants this legitimate concession which is being requested from every corner of the house, we shall be glad to give him every support.

Undoubtedly a case has been made out for these young men, but one factor has been understated if it has been stated at all. When these men entered into this employment at a comparatively high rate of remuneration the income tax was relatively low, but the tax to-day, applied to a man making $900 a month or whatever it is, is a very severe tax. I hope the minister will give consideration to the request that is being made on behalf of these men. I happen to have met some of them, and I know they feel that they really have a just grievance in view of the very high rate of income tax. The British government induced the Americans to come over here, and I was talking to one of them when we were flying across. They are indemnified against the imposition of income tax. But the Canadian government has not done that with respect to our residents here, and of course there is a measure of discrimination there. Just what proposal would be just and fair, I am not prepared to say, but I think a case has been made out for some concession to these men. They are engaged in a very hazardous occupation; there is no question about that. Outside of actual combat in the air I do not know of any more hazardous occupation than flying on the bomber command.
Income War Tax

I should like to
lend my voice in support of those who have spoken on behalf of these men who are flying on the bomber command. It may be said that they went into it with their eyes open, but they will be engaged on this hazardous work for only a short time and they have to provide for their families. Theirs is an occupation as hazardous as there is in the world to-day.
There are some other inequities. We have in Canada on the east coast and on the west coast troops who have enlisted for active service. Some of these troops may be located on a lonely island, where they are shut off from everything. Perhaps a little distance away on a boat in the harbour are some naval officers whose incomes are exempt from taxation because they are afloat. The men of whom I am speaking, located in some lonely spot, and who are liable tO' be called for service anywhere at any moment, find that their incomes are not exempt from taxation.
We have other troops who have enlisted for active service and are located somewhere along the border in Canada. Right across the border in the United States or in Alaska there are other troops, and our soldiers see a discrimination there in the matter of income tax.
Some concession in the matter of income tax exemption should be granted to these men who have enlisted for active service and are located in some lonely post. They should have the same exemption as those who are located just outside Canada. Surely some scheme could be worked out to remove the present cause of discontent. Troops who are serving on the east coast or away up in Labrador are just as much on active service there as troops in the Yukon or Alaska or Newfoundland, and they feel that there is a great deal of discrimination under the present circumstances.

This is the first time I have taken part in the discussions of the income tax resolutions, and as I have listened to what has gone on now for a considerable time, I have frequently wondered where the taxes are to come from or who is to pay them. Nevertheless I think this is a case to which the minister should' give very serious consideration. One point which has not been mentioned is that our Royal Canadian Air Force flyers in Canada who have more than 400 hours of operational flying are, I understand, exempt from income tax. This ferry flying 'is undoubtedly more dangerous than operational flying in Canada, and I am sure that the exemption of the men engaged in

it would be well received everywhere. As far as other civilians are concerned, those of us who are getting a reasonable standard of living have no reason to complain of the taxes we are asked to pay, and would have no complaint even though they were higher. So far, after all, we have not sacrificed anything. I trust the minister will give favourable consideration to this request.

I rise primarily for the purpose of joining those who have pleaded so eloquently and convincingly for the men serving in the ferry and bomber commands. In my own constituency one of our finest boys, a member of the ferry command, lost his life some months ago. I knew something about his case, and I have taken close interest in the details of the hazardous and dangerous job to which hese men are assigned. I would simply add a word to what has been said in favour of exempting them from this taxation. In a period of war we must not lose our sense of relative values. Many men and women to-day are doing extremely hazardous work, and although some may not be as close to the scene of battle as others, the danger is there.
I think the minister might also reconsider the matter of the legislation he proposes to bring down based upon resolution 22. This seems to me to go only part way to meet the situation which has developed.
