Perhaps we might regularize the proceedings by my simply closing my remarks with respect to the matter to which I was referring a moment ago, and reserving what I have to say until resolution 22 and the amendments which the minister is apparently intending to bring down are before the committee, because they may alter the _ whole structure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand' it, we are on resolution 30, which is the one relating to the merchant marine; at least, I gave notice of the moving of that resolution. I am not clear about the procedure: I thought all I had to do was to move the resolution and discuss it. But apparently resolution 30 is to be reached later; yet discussion has been permitted, to which I take no objection, on that resolution; and because the matter of the ferry command is connected with the subject of the merchant marine, several hon. members have asked that some consideration be given to exempting from income taxation part of the salaries of the members of the ferry command. I may say that consideration is being given to that proposal, and later I will communicate to the committee the decision of the government. It is a matter which does not have to be dealt with by resolution because, if anything is done, it would be an alleviation of taxation rather than an imposition of taxation.
I just wish to remind the committee that the fact that we exempt certain persons from income tax and partly relieve others from income tax creates tremendous difficulties for the government and for the departments of Finance and National Revenue, because the moment an exemption is given to one particular class, the demand is made that it be extended to a somewhat similar class. Last year I was rigid in my position that we should not extend any exemptions beyond those who were members of the armed forces. Yet the case of the merchant seamen presents such a tremendous appeal to the sympathies, and not only that, but the merchant seamen are doing such remarkable work, work so necessary for the defence of our country and for the carrying on of the war, that it is very difficult to be deaf to their requests. Those requests for the most part, I may say, are based upon a dislike of discrimination more than upon a desire to escape taxation. Possibly, if we had followed the English rule, which is to tax all residents of the United
Kingdom regardless of whether they are in the forces or out of the forces, whether they are on the seas or off the seas, whether they are in the air or on the ground, there would not have been very much complaint. But we took the other course.
Are there no exemptions on these grounds?-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have never heard of any
exemptions at all. This is the situation that exists. Members of our navy sometimes will be serving in the same ship with members of the British navy. The members of the British navy will have a very large proportion of their pay taken in taxation, while the members of our forces serving on the same ship will not be taxed at all. In Great Britain the members of the British forces will be subject to taxation; the members of our forces will not be subject to taxation at all. I presume the members of this ferry command who are residents of the United Kingdom are subject to United Kingdom taxation.

If they are on this
side they are given a living allowance which brings their pay up considerably, to help them meet that obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I see; they get a special
allowance, but they are subject to United Kingdom taxation. So that these requests create almost intolerable problems, because the moment one is granted it leads to another. As a matter of fact, the appearance of the merchant marine resolution on the order paper immediately caused representatives of the ferry command to come to Ottawa and say they should be treated as well as the merchant marine.
They were here before that, though, were they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; they were, but this
caused them to renew their representations in a much more emphatic manner than ever before. All I can say is that with regard to the merchant marine this is a concession as far as part of it is concerned, namely, the meals and so on. That is not based on any principle at all; it is just a concession to the merchant marine, and I just wish the committee to appreciate the great difficulties of the taxing authorities in drawing lines, because- we are driven from position to position.
After having said all that and having made my appeal for such sympathy as it may be possible to get, I wish to say that we are giving consideration to the representations of the ferry command.

Income War Tax

I hope they will be
favourable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, that remains to be
seen.
I suggest that we now take up resolution 14 which was allowed to stand.
* 14. That the tax payable by a corporation shall be paid by twelve monthly instalments commencing in the sixth month prior to the close of its fiscal period
(a)	as to the first eleven months, one-twelfth of the estimated tax, having regard to the previous or anticipated current year's income, applying the current year's rates, and
(b)	as to the twelfth month, the balance of the tax payable, having regard to the income and applying the rates of the taxation year;
provided, however, that should any instalment paid in each month of the seventh to eleventh month, both inclusive, be less than one-twelfth of the tax actually found to have been due, such deficiencjr shall bear interest at the rate of 5 per cent per annum from the close of the company's fiscal period.

As I recall the situation, the Minister of National Revenue had made some amendments to this resolution but had not gone through the formality of having the amendments brought to the attention of the committee in the usual way.

At first we thought a change might be necessitated here, but the resolution as it stands will be the foundation for the section in the act, though we are going to make a concession to the taxpayer in this way, that if he pays on the basis of the previous year's income no interest will be payable for the six months prior to the end of his fiscal year.

I do not wish to raise any unnecessary questions about this, but resolution No. 14 has been changed; it has been altered; it has been amended, actually, and if the resolution meant what it said in the first instance then it cannot mean the same thing now. It is very difficult for me to follow the line of reasoning of the Minister of National Revenue, who says that if not the principle then the details in connection with the resolution are to be altered, but still there is to be no amendment to the resolution itself. The minister should make it a little clearer than that.

The only point was that if there were to be any increase in the tax there would1 have to be an amendment. There is not to be an increase; as a matter of fact, if anything there will be a decrease in the tax on account of the fact that no interest will be charged on those payments which were worked out on the basis of the previous year's income.
 *

Then may I ask the minister if, when the bill itself is brought before the house, the appropriate section will have an exact relationship to the terms of the resolution, or whether it will be changed?
It will be in the same relationship to the terms of this resolution.

If that is the case, it does not make very much difference what the resolution calls for. I am not going to block the passing of this resolution, but I wish to protest against what I think is a very irregular sort of procedure. If, however, the minister wants to take the responsibility in connection with it, I suppose I should1 not object further.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is the irregularity? I understood the minister to say that the section would follow the resolution, which to my knowledge has not been amended. I was out of the chamber part of the time, but this resolution stood in order that it might be examined with a view to determining whether or not an amendment was necessary. No amendment is deemed necessary. I thought the situation was that the section would either follow the resolution or impose a burden less than that imposed by the resolution. That was what I took to be the situation, and I think that is correct.
I find it a little hard, without remembering the terms of the act which was passed last year, to determine exactly the effect of this resolution, but I think it is this. The tax is payable by a corporation beginning in the middle of its fiscal year, and that payment continues for twelve months; that is, the last six months of the current fiscal year and the first six months of the following fiscal year. I understand that in the present act some interest is provided for underpayments during the first six months, but that this imposed a higher rate, really, for the six months beyond the end of the fiscal year, because the 5 per cent applies from the end of the fiscal year even,if the deficiency arises after the end of the fiscal year. I understand that the act will either follow that exactly or lighten that to some extent. It is not a very big matter one way or the other, but that is the situation. I do not think there is anything irregular. It may be that hon. members shou.ld watch closely the section of the act, and if we start trying to jack up any taxes that would be irregular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I read it earlier in the evening. It is an administrative matter, a formal matter. The hon. member for York-Sunbury listened attentively when I read it; he did not agree with it, but he seemed to agree that it was merely an administrative matter.
We have never had an opportunity of seeing the resolution. I do not wish to ask impossible things, but it seems to me we ought to see these resolutions before we pass them.

We are not going to be able to pass all these resolutions to-night. It might stand so that we may have a chance at least to look at it.
Resolution stands.
30. That any amount received by an officer or man of the merchant marine as bona fide war risk bonus in accordance with the usage of the merchant marine, and any value of board or lodging on shipboard received by such a person while performing services in respect of which war risk bonus is payable shall not be considered as income subject to tax under the Income War Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I give the committee notice that there may be some slight changes in the bill, but the principle of the resolution will be
observed. There may be some method of ascertaining the extent of the war risk bonus in cases in which it might not otherwise be ascertained. That would be one thing.
Unfortunately I was not in the committee at the time the hon. member for Comox-Albemi spoke. No doubt he dealt with this at some length.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; he talked about the ferry command.
What is actually meant by "bona fide war risk bonus in accordance with the usage of the merchant marine"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think they receive a special payment in certain areas, called the war risk bonus; that is those who are subject to salary and wage control. The bonuses are subject to approval by some governmental body here; I think it is the national war labour board.

Has it the force of a
statute, or a regulation, or an order in council, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot answer those questions. By to-morrow afternoon I shall be much more definite. If hon. members wish to get more definite information as to the authority under which it is paid and the degree of control there is in governmental agencies here I would have to get more definite information than I have at present. But I thought it was safe to pass the resolution because I am not going to depart from the principle of it.
This does not mean that the full pay of the merchant marine is being exempted from taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; it does not.
Some'hon. MEMBERS: Carried.

I thought the minister
wanted to amend this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I do not think any
amendment will be necessary.
Mr. GRAYDON-: Is this "bona fide war risk bonus in accordance with the usage of the merchant marine" a substantial amount or a very small proportion of the amount received by the ordinary seaman? If it is only a small proportion, this exemption from income tax on it is rather futile. My view has always been that the merchant marine is about the most hazardous occupation a man can follow in war time under present conditions. I do not wish to enlarge on that, but I do not know of any job outside perhaps one or two of a similar nature that is more hazardous. It
Privilege-Mr. Graydon

seems to me that if the exemption is to be for only a small portion of the actual amount received by seamen who make these perilous trips, it does not go far enough, and I would not feel like letting the resolution go through without further debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let it stand, then. It is
substantial. I will get the information.

If the minister is prepared to indicate that it is a substantial amount, and a worth-while concession, I shall have no objection to the resolution passing. I do not wish to hold it up, and that is not my object. But if it is just a small amount I would not be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might better stand until
to-morrow.
Resolution 30 stands.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, April 16, 1943
